references.text: Abraham hurried to prepare a calf for his guests, a parallel to the fattened calf that is slaughtered to celebrate the son's return ([ref:Gen 18:7-8|Genesis 18:7-8]).
Isaiah describes the messianic feast that the Lord prepares for all peoples, with rich dishes – a parallel to the joy and celebration with the fattened calf ([ref:Isa 25:6|Isaiah 25:6]).

The following verse explains the reason for the feast: the son was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found – this gives meaning to the slaughter of the fattened calf ([ref:Luk 15:24|Luke 15:24]).
The joy over finding the lost sheep and the invitation to rejoice together parallels the joy over the prodigal son's return, expressed through a feast ([ref:Luk 15:6-7|Luke 15:6-7]).
The woman who found the lost coin called friends and neighbors together to rejoice – the same pattern of communal joy as the celebration with the fattened calf ([ref:Luk 15:9-10|Luke 15:9-10]).
Levi held a great feast for Jesus, a parallel to the meal expressing joy in God's presence ([ref:Luk 5:29|Luke 5:29]).
The marriage supper of the Lamb in Revelation is the ultimate celebration of reunion between God and his people, which the fattened calf points toward ([ref:Rev 19:7-9|Revelation 19:7-9]).

In the Mosaic Law, feasts are encouraged with purchased food and drink before the Lord, where one may rejoice – a background for the joyful celebration with the fattened calf ([ref:Deut 14:26|Deuteronomy 14:26]).

The woman at Endor prepared a fattened calf for Saul – the same expression (μόσχος σιτευτός in the LXX) is used for a special calf kept back for an important occasion ([ref:1 Sam 28:24-25|1 Samuel 28:24-25]).
